subtopics.title: From Raw Data to a Frequency Table

questions.question: Using intervals 0–<20, 20–<40, 40–<60, 60–<80, 80–<100 minutes, a learner who worked exactly 40 minutes is tallied into:
options: the 20-to-40 class
the 40-to-60 class — each interval includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper one
both classes, half each
whichever class has fewer entries

questions.question: The frequencies are 6, 16, 9, 6 and 3. The audit that must be run before anything else is:
options: checking that 16 is the largest
converting each frequency to a percentage
confirming 6 + 16 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 40, the number of learners
checking the intervals are in alphabetical order

questions.question: Homework times are organised into class intervals rather than listed value by value because:
options: continuous measured data is summarised by grouping it into equal-width intervals that cover everything
tables are only allowed five rows
learners dislike exact numbers
intervals make the mean larger

questions.question: In the completed histogram, the bar on the 20-to-40 interval:
options: rises to height 16 — the tallest bar
rises to height 9
spans 20 to 60
is drawn separated from its neighbours

questions.question: A histogram's bars touch because:
options: it saves space on the page
the data is continuous — 39,9 minutes flows into 40,0 with nothing between them
the frequencies are all different
touching bars are easier to shade

questions.question: The display that DOES use gaps between bars is:
options: any graph of times or masses
a histogram with small frequencies
a bar graph of categories — like favourite subjects — because nothing exists between the categories
a frequency table

subtopics.title: Reading the Shape — Mode, Middle and Skew

questions.question: The modal class of the homework data is:
options: 40 to below 60 minutes
20 to below 40 minutes, holding 16 of the 40 learners
0 to below 20 minutes
80 to below 100 minutes

questions.question: With cumulative counts 6, 22, 31, 37, 40, the median class is found by:
options: locating the 20th and 21st values — both sit in the 20-to-40 class
picking the middle interval of the five
averaging the smallest and largest values
choosing the class with frequency closest to 20

questions.question: The estimated mean uses midpoints 10, 30, 50, 70, 90 and gives:
options: 1 680 ÷ 5 = 336 minutes
40 ÷ 5 = 8 minutes

questions.question: This histogram climbs quickly, peaks on 20-to-40, then trails right through 9, 6 and 3. Its shape is:
options: skewed to the left, because the peak sits on the left
symmetrical
skewed to the right — skew is named after the tail's direction, and the long tail points right
bimodal

questions.question: The three slots of a full analysis comment are:
options: centre, spread, shape
mean, median, mode
title, axes, bars
minimum, maximum, total

questions.question: Which centre sentence would earn the most credit?
options: 'The data has a centre.'
'The modal class is 20 to below 40 minutes and the estimated mean is 42, so a typical learner spends around forty minutes on homework.'
'The mean is a number in the middle.'
'Most bars are tall.'

questions.question: Asked about the limitations of this grouped display, a top answer notes that:
options: histograms cannot show frequencies above 20
the graph would improve with gaps between bars
forty learners is always too small a sample
it reveals no learner's exact time and cannot explain WHY some learners work longer — grouping trades detail for overview

questions.question: In the pigeonhole picture, a slip reading exactly 40 minutes is posted into:
options: the forty-to-sixty hole — every hole keeps its bottom number and refuses its top one
the twenty-to-forty hole
either hole, poster's choice
a special boundary hole

questions.question: 'Count the counts' means:
options: counting how many pigeonholes there are
adding the slips in each hole — 6 + 16 + 9 + 6 + 3 — and confirming the total matches the forty slips posted
counting the slips twice for safety
recounting only the fullest hole

questions.question: The boundary rule works like data bundles on a phone because:
options: both involve money
phone bundles use histograms
the moment a value reaches the next threshold it belongs to the next bracket — no value sits in two brackets
both round values to the nearest ten

subtopics.title: The Mountain Range Tells the Story

questions.question: In the mountain-range reading of the histogram, the summit over 20-to-40 tells you:
options: those learners work hardest
the range is drawn incorrectly
homework gets easier after 40 minutes
that is where the homework times crowd — the most common bracket

questions.question: 'Tall means many, wide means nothing' warns that:
options: only a bar's height counts learners — every bar is twenty minutes wide by construction
wide bars hold more learners
bars should be drawn as thin as possible
height and width both measure frequency

questions.question: Cricket versus hockey participation is drawn with separated towers because:
options: sports data is always small
the data is categories — nothing lives between cricket and hockey — so the display is a bar graph with gaps
separated towers are taller
the minutes line is unbroken

questions.question: The three questions that generate the full comment are:
options: Who collected it? When? Where?
Where is the crowd? How scattered are they? Is the range lopsided?
What is the title? What are the units? How many bars?
Is it a histogram? Is it a bar graph? Is it a table?

questions.question: 'Skewed right' alone scores less than 'a few learners work very long evenings while most finish quickly' because:
options: shorter answers always score less
skew should never be mentioned
interpreting means returning the numbers to the real situation they came from
the second sentence uses more words

questions.question: When comparing two histograms, a valid comparison pairs:
options: one graph's centre against the other's spread
the tallest bar of one against the total of the other
the title of one against the axes of the other
crowd against crowd, scatter against scatter, ridge against ridge — like with like
